did_you_know.text: Did you know? Ezekiel is commanded to take a brick and engrave a depiction of Jerusalem on it. In this way, he creates a visual illustration of the prophecy concerning the city’s fate.

Did you know? Around the model of Jerusalem, Ezekiel is instructed to portray a siege using a siege ramp, a mound, camps, and battering rams—measures described in the verse as part of the attack on the city.

Did you know? Ezekiel places an iron griddle between himself and the model of the city and faces it as though it were under siege. The verse explicitly identifies this action as a sign to the house of Israel.
Did you know? Ezekiel is instructed to lie on his left side and bear the guilt of the house of Israel. The length of time he lies there is meant to represent the years of their guilt in days.

Did you know? After 390 days on his left side, Ezekiel is commanded to lie on his right side for 40 days and bear the guilt of the house of Judah. The verse explains the principle: one day represents one year.

Did you know? During this symbolic act, Ezekiel is instructed to face the siege of Jerusalem, bare his arm, and prophesy against it. Both his posture and his facing the city are part of the prophetic message.

Did you know? Ezekiel is described as having ropes placed upon him, and he is not allowed to turn from one side to the other until he has completed the days of the siege. This emphasizes the compulsion and fixed nature of the symbolic act.

Did you know? The bread Ezekiel must prepare is made from six kinds of grain and legumes: wheat, barley, beans, lentils, millet, and spelt. He is instructed to put them all in one vessel and eat the bread for 390 days.

Did you know? The bread is to be baked in an unusual way, using human dung, in the sight of the people. When Ezekiel objects on grounds of ritual purity, the Lord allows him to use cattle dung instead.

Did you know? At the end of the chapter, the meaning of these actions is explained: in Jerusalem, the staff of bread will be broken, and the people will eat bread by weight and drink water by measure—a picture of scarcity, anxiety, and ruin.
